Cybersecurity industry experts study and rank all the methods by which organizations get hacked, and among the top vectors of attack is social engineering.

![[people-world-map-work-area-blue.jpg]]

## Understand Social Engineering in the Wild


Social engineering is a psychological manipulation tactic used to trick individuals into divulging confidential or personal information that can be used for fraudulent purposes. It's a common method used in cybersecurity breaches. Social engineering exploits human emotions, such as trust, fear, or curiosity, rather than relying solely on technical hacking techniques.

  

It is among [the most common types of cyberattacks](https://secureframe.com/hub/grc/most-common-types-of-cyberattacks) that is used by cyber attackers to exploit potential victims.

  

Why is social engineering attack dangerous threat for companies? Because it contains a human element. Usually mistakes are made by legitimate users and it is difficult to detect, predict and remediate. In many cases victims don't even realize that they have been tricked. 

  

Basically there are four steps the attacker takes to gain access to sensitive data. Of course, there are many scenarios how attackers can achieve their goals, but these steps are most common and should be known about. 

  

  
  

#### Step 1: Research. 

  

The bad actor is running a research of a potential victim or group of victims: jobs, hobbies, and other personal information. 

  

#### Step 2: Hook.

  

The attacker contacts a target and tries to establish a trusting relationship using researched information.

  

#### Step 3: Play.

  

The attacker manipulates the victim using different techniques but most commonly psychological methods that we are going to talk about a little later, to reveal sensitive data or perform a specific action. 

  

#### Step 4: Exit.

  

After getting necessary information or requested action, the attacker stops communication.

## Social Engineering Attack Examples 

#### Jaguar / Land Rover Attack

According to the experts at the Cyber Monitoring Centre (CMC), [the most economically damaging cyber event in UK history](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cy9pdld4y81o) is the Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) cyberattack that happened in August 2025. The estimated cost was £1.9bn. 

The attack caused the production fall out of the car giant's production starting September 1 for five weeks and caused widespread delays across JLR's supply chain. About 5,000 businesses have been affected in total and a full recovery will not be reached until January 2026. 

Even though JLR hasn’t published any post-mortem report about the cyber attack, the researchers think [the hackers executed well-known tactics](https://treblle.com/blog/jlr-breach-breakdown-analysis): social engineering, credential abuse, weak segmentation, and inadequate detection. 

Talking about social engineering, investigations suggest the breach originated from a targeted vishing campaign weeks earlier, when attackers posing as internal staff tricked employees into disclosing credentials.

  
#### Stuxnet Attack 
  
[Stuxnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuxnet) was introduced through an infected USB flash drive, allowing it to cross that air gap and enter the target environment. Once inside, it spread through Windows systems, searched for Siemens Step7 software, and only activated when it found the specific industrial setup it was designed to sabotage.

The human factor matters because someone had to bring the infected device or equipment into the environment. What is assumed to have occurred is that an Iranian mole working for Dutch intelligence inserted the virus using a USB drive, or convinced someone at Natanz to do it. It's also speculated that infected USB drives from contractors could have helped the malware reach systems not accessible through the internet.

So, in a social engineering context, Stuxnet shows a different model: not tricking a user online, but exploiting trust in insiders, contractors, removable media, and physical access to bridge the gap between the outside world and a protected industrial network.

#### Bangladesh Bank Heist 
  

[The Bangladesh Bank cyberheist began](https://www.csoonline.com/article/4131864/10-years-later-bangladesh-bank-cyberheist-still-offers-cyber-resiliency-lessons.html) with a human-facing entry point: spear-phishing emails sent to bank employees in late 2015 or earlier. 

Those emails carried malware, and once opened or enabled, they allowed the attackers to plant a backdoor inside the bank’s internal network. From there, the attackers quietly mapped the environment, identified SWIFT-connected systems, and moved toward the bank’s international money-transfer workflow.

The attackers were later linked to North Korea’s Lazarus Group. Their goal was not just to break into a system, but to abuse trusted financial processes. After gaining access, they obtained valid SWIFT operator credentials, compromised databases, and even sabotaged the printer that produced SWIFT transaction logs so staff would not immediately see what was happening. 

They then sent 35 fraudulent SWIFT payment instructions attempting to steal $951 million from Bangladesh Bank’s account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Only five transactions succeeded, but that was still enough to move $81 million through accounts in the Philippines before the money was laundered through casinos.

So the social-engineering angle is clear: the breach started by targeting employees with spear-phishing, then escalated into credential theft, workflow manipulation, and abuse of trusted banking channels.


### Takeaways


Why are social engineering attacks still dominating among other attacks and people still get tricked even if they heard about it and read cyber news? 

The answer is simple: attackers use psychological methods on their potential victims to achieve their desired goals. It is trust and authority, urgency and scarcity, curiosity etc.  

When we panic, we become vulnerable, stop thinking rationally and therefore make mistakes. In our next section you will learn how attackers leverage social engineering using psychological angles.

## Types of social engineering attacks


Social engineering attacks can take various forms and utilize different methods to deceive and exploit individuals. Let's discuss the most prevalent forms of such attacks.

The first four attacks are different types of phishing attacks, but before going deep into the details, let’s clarify what phishing means. 

**Phishing** is an attempt to steal personal information or break into online accounts using deceptive emails, messages, ads, or sites that look similar to sites you already use. The first phishing attack we are going to talk about is a phishing email. 
<br>
<br>


### Phishing Emails:

I am sure, at least once you have received a strange email from a bank or insurance company with a request to send them your address, personal identification number or a phone number, because due to some systems updating clients’ personal information should be checked manually. Sounds ridiculous, right? 

Attackers usually send emails that appear to be from legitimate sources, using urgent language and directing recipients to fake websites where their personal information can be harvested or asking to verify personal information via email. 

#### Example - FACC

You will be shocked by the example of the successful phishing attack that happened at the [Austrian aerospace parts manufacturer FACC](https://www.reuters.com/article/us-facc-ceo-idUSKCN0YG0ZF) in 2016. An employee has received an email with a request to transfer €42 million to another account as part of an “acquisition project”. 

This email was sent by the CEO of the company, Walter Stephan, but in fact it was a scam. And you know what? The employee has transferred money. The CEO and the employee were fired afterwards. So, before implementing any requests that are sent by email, it is better to double check by simply calling the sender. 

#### Example - Scoular

[The Scoular](https://www.scoular.com/), a giant grain company, was a target of the whaling attack in 2015. Everything was according to the ideal phishing attack scenario: the Scoular’s corporate controller [received a fake email](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/email-scam-netted-17-million-from) from the CEO saying that they needed to transfer $17.2 million to China. 

The corporate controller was not alerted by this email, because he knew that the company was talking about expansion towards China. The controller even called the accountant’s phone number written in the email and talked to the fake accountant. The transfer was made and the company lost $17.2 million. 
<br>
<br>

### Spear Phishing:


Similar to phishing but more targeted, these attacks are customized to the individual, often including personal information to seem more credible. Let’s discuss a few types of spear phishing:  business email compromise and whaling. 

#### Business Email compromise

In business email compromise the attacker impersonates himself to someone you know from your company: a colleague, CEO or vendor). In these emails the sender requests making money transfers, changing bank details for the future payments. Usually this type of spear phishing aims for financial loss for the company. 

#### Example - Quanta Computer

For example, between 2013 and 2015, the Lithuanian citizen [Evaldas Rimasauskas](https://www.techworm.net/2019/03/man-facebook-google-fake-invoices.html) impersonated a Taiwanese hardware supplier, Quanta Computer. This company provided services that were used by two tech giants, Google and Facebook. 

He sent out fake invoices worth $122 million ($99 million and $23 million to Google and Facebook, respectively) to these companies for almost three years. He was arrested and imprisoned for 30 years.
<br>
<br>

### Whaling: 

Whaling is a type of spear phishing where the target is a “big fish” - a “whale” in the company. Usually the main target of the attack is a senior employee like the CEO, or General Director of the company. Senior employees have access to sensitive information of the company, and if leaked it could hit business very badly. 

#### Example - Seagate

In 2016 the technology company Seagate [was tricked into releasing the W2 forms of 10,000 employees](https://www.fortinet.com/resources/cyberglossary/whaling-attack). This is an ideal form of the whaling attack: it involved an email that requested copies of the employees’ 2016 W-2 forms, moreover, other sensitive information such as their Social Security numbers, names, home addresses, and income. When HR complied, the information was sent straight into cyber criminals' hands.
<br>
<br>

### Vishing (Voice Phishing):


Vishing involves phone calls where the attacker impersonates legitimate entities, attempting to obtain sensitive information or influence the recipient to perform specific actions. 

#### Example

[According to Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/jessedamiani/2019/09/03/a-voice-deepfake-was-used-to-scam-a-ceo-out-of-243000/?sh=22e3dc952241), in 2019 the CEO of an unnamed UK-based energy company believed he received a call from his boss, a chief executive from a German parent company, requesting to transfer 220.000 euro to a bank account of a Hungarian supplier. 

The attacker used an AI voice technology to fake the German chief executive. During the investigation, the CEO said he noticed the German accent and carried the man’s “melody”. The money was sent to the attacker.
<br>
<br>

### Smishing (SMS Phishing):


In smishing attacks SMS messages are used to distribute phishing links or encourage recipients to share personal information, often using urgent language to prompt quick action. 

Well, I am going to tell you a story that happened to me when I studied at the university. 

It was December, I successfully passed all exams and was about to go home to visit my parents. They lived in another city that was about 1500 km away from the city I studied. 

At that time I saved money for Christmas presents and was in the process of buying different nice things for my family. At the end of the day, I had all the presents except for my dad. 

And here comes smishing! I received an SMS saying that I have won a phone and if I want to take it I had to pay a certain amount of money (not a lot, but for a student, each penny was a treasure). 

And what do you think I did? I was so happy and already imagined how my dad would be surprised to get a new phone for Christmas, and I transferred money to the sender.

Then I received one more message, saying that I would get my phone, but I had to pay for the delivery. I was lucky enough not to have enough money, and of course I didn’t send any. 

Then, I found out that it was a primitive version of smishing. How could I fall for it? You see, what emotions can do to a person! Well, anyway the lesson is learned. 
<br>
<br>

### Pretexting:

In Pretexting the attackers create a fabricated scenario or pretext to interact with the target, with the goal of extracting information or gaining certain privileges. They may impersonate coworkers, police officers, bank officials, etc. 

#### Example - Family pressure

One of the emotionally triggering pretexting attacks is when a grandparent receives a phone call from a grandchild. An AI generated voice saying that the grandchild is in trouble and the grandparent needs to pay money to get his grandchild back. Of course, during such a phone call, an average person would panic and do everything possible to help their beloved ones. 
<br>
<br>

### Baiting:

In baiting, the attacker promises something enticing to the victim, like free software, only to deliver malware or other malicious content. The most common example is downloading free music, games or a movie that contains malware. 
<br>
<br>

### USB Drops:

USB drops is one type of baiting. Malicious USB drives are left in locations where targets can find them, relying on human curiosity to insert them into computers, which then deploy malware.

#### Example - BadUSB

In January 2022, the FBI issued a warning saying that members for [a Russian cyber criminal group named FIN7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIN7) have been targeting transportation and insurance companies and defense companies with BadUSB attacks designed to deliver REvil and or BlackMatter ransomware. 

The USB drives were sent to targets in packages claiming to be from Amazon or the United States Department of Health and Human Services with letters about free gift cards or COVID-19 protocols that are placed on USB drives. Of course, after plugging in the USB drives malware was automatically downloaded. 
<br>
<br>

### Quid Pro Quo Attacks:

Here, the attacker offers something in return for the target’s information or action, creating a false sense of reciprocal obligation. For example, you have a problem with your laptop. You contact an IT company explaining the problem. 

Afterwards, they say they will help you for free because it is a minor issue, not even a problem, but they can do it only if you give a remote access to your laptop. It means, they will have remote access to all your files. Nobody does something for free, remember that. 
<br>
<br>

### Tailgating or Piggybacking:

Attackers physically follow authorized personnel into secure areas, exploiting the polite tendency of individuals to hold doors open for others. When I worked at the office, I remember myself “helping” colleagues, but it is not right. 
<br>
<br>

### Waterholing:


Waterholing is the attack when attackers compromise websites frequently visited by their targets and use them to deliver malware, anticipating that the targets will eventually visit the compromised site. To be honest, I find this attack very creative!

#### Example - Marriot hotels

[In 2018 the Marriott Hotel faced](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/exploring-infamous-watering-hole-attacks-recent-history-abed-a-a-/) a data breach. It is a high-profile example of a watering hole attack that caused significant damage. Personal information of over 500 million Marriott guests was compromised, including their names, addresses, phone numbers, passport numbers, and credit card information. 

In this case, the source of the malware was a vendor’s website. The vendor was a company that managed Marriott's reservation systems, and the attackers could use this connection to gain access to Marriott's networks.
<br>
<br>

### Social Media Manipulation:

Attackers use social media platforms to disseminate misinformation, impersonate individuals, or use harvested information for targeted attacks. 

### Scareware

Scareware is a type of social engineering that uses fear to trick users into downloading malware, paying for fake services, or giving up personal information. 

It typically presents itself as fake security alerts, pop-ups, or messages that claim a user's device is infected or at risk. These tactics are designed to create panic, pressuring users to act immediately by purchasing worthless software or providing access to their systems. 

#### Example - WinFixer

One of the scareware programs is [WinFixer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WinFixer). It was a group of scareware rogue security programs created by Winsoftware, falsely claiming to fix system issues on Microsoft Windows computers once users purchased the full version. 

In most cases, the software was installed without the user’s knowledge or consent. McAfee claimed that “the primary function of the free version appears to be to alarm the user into paying for registration, at least partially based on false or erroneous detections”. The program urged users to buy a paid version of the software.

Many sources reported that the program actually decreased system stability and performance. The associated websites were shut down in December 2008 following intervention by the Federal Trade Commission.
<br>
<br>

## Takeaways

There are many more cyber attacks used to get sensitive information and/or earn money. Cyber attackers are very creative and innovative. 

When receiving a message or phone call and you find it suspicious, just hang up and call back to the organization or person you talked to. Talk to your family members and make up a secret word for emergencies that only you know and if something happens, use this word as a password so you know that person you are talking to is real, not a pretender with an AI generated voice.
